paragraphs.heading: Galaxies without a set shape
paragraphs.text: An irregular galaxy is one with no clear, regular shape, unlike a spiral or an elliptical. It fits none of the regular classes of the Hubble sequence and often looks chaotic, with no central bulge and no trace of spiral arms. Other galaxies show an axis of symmetry in how their blue light is spread, but irregulars have none. Taken together, irregulars are thought to be about a quarter of all galaxies.

paragraphs.heading: How they get that way
paragraphs.text: Irregulars arise in several ways. Some were once spirals or ellipticals that an uneven outside gravitational pull bent out of shape, and some may be young galaxies between spiral and elliptical status. Galaxy collisions can also make them. They are commonly small, about a tenth of the Milky Way's mass, and their small size leaves them open to run-ins with large galaxies and intergalactic clouds. Some, especially the Magellanic type, are small spirals being pulled out of shape by the gravity of a larger neighbour.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of irregular
paragraphs.text: Astronomers split irregulars into kinds. An Irr I galaxy shows some structure, but not enough to place it cleanly in the Hubble sequence. An Irr II galaxy shows no structure that could place it there, and is often shaped by a collision or merger. A dwarf irregular, or dIrr, is an irregular with a luminosity below 10⁸L_(⊙). Irregulars make up a large share of the Local Group, and most of those are distant dwarf irregulars.

paragraphs.heading: Windows on early galaxies
paragraphs.text: Dwarf irregulars are now thought to matter for understanding how galaxies change over time. They tend to be low in metals and fairly rich in gas, and they are thought to resemble the earliest galaxies in the Universe. They may be a nearby, and so more recent, version of the faint blue galaxies seen in deep field surveys. They also hold large amounts of dark matter.

paragraphs.heading: Where stars are born
paragraphs.text: With so little structure, irregulars have few density waves, the patterns believed to help star formation along in spirals. That makes them good places to study star birth without that effect. Star formation in them is common and varied, and some form stars at rates comparable to spirals. The process itself is the same as in other galaxies, but it may be driven more by gas moving at random, by massive stars and by giant HII regions, which are unusually common in them.

paragraphs.heading: The Magellanic Clouds
paragraphs.text: The Magellanic Clouds show how these labels can shift. Both were once classed as irregular galaxies. The Large Magellanic Cloud has since been reclassified as type SBm, a barred Magellanic spiral. The Small Magellanic Cloud is still classed as an irregular, type Im, even though it does have a bar.
